topics.ch: A Letter to God (poems: Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice)
topics.t: Faith of a farmer: reading and determiners
topics.h: One hailstorm can flatten a whole field in ten minutes. What keeps a farmer going the next morning?
p: 'A Letter to God' is about a poor farmer whose crop is ruined by hail; his faith stays so strong that he writes a letter to God asking for help.
Literal questions are answered by words in the text; inference questions need clues, like a smile after a disaster showing hope.
Faith means complete trust; a person with faith expects help even when things look bad.
Determiners come before nouns: a, an, the, this, some, each, many, much, few, little.
Use many and few with countable nouns (many seeds, few clouds); use much and little with uncountable nouns (much water, little rain).

ex.q: Passage: After the hailstorm, Hari's cotton field lay flat. His children cried, but Hari looked at the sky and smiled, 'Help will come.' Next morning he borrowed seeds and sowed again. What does Hari's smile tell us about him?
st: His field is destroyed and his children are crying, so the situation is very bad.
Yet he smiles and says 'Help will come', so he is not giving up.
He also sows again the next day, which proves his hope is real.
ex.a: Hari has deep faith and hope; he trusts that help will come and acts on that trust.

topics.rl: When a crop fails, many farmers in Maharashtra, Punjab or Odisha replant with seeds shared by neighbours. Faith and community help them start again.

topics.ch: A Letter to God (poems: Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice)
topics.t: Irony: when the opposite happens
topics.h: A fire station catching fire. A traffic policeman getting a challan. Why do these make us smile?
p: Irony is a contrast between what is expected and what actually happens or is meant.
Verbal irony: saying the opposite of what you mean, e.g. 'Lovely weather!' during a storm. Sarcasm is a sharp form of verbal irony.
Situational irony: the result is the opposite of what was expected.
Dramatic irony: the audience or reader knows something a character does not.
In 'A Letter to God', the farmer calls the post office staff 'crooks', though they are the very people who collected money to help him.

ex.q: Meena's brother laughed at her for carrying an umbrella on a sunny morning in Kochi. By noon, it poured, and he had to beg to share it. What kind of irony is this?
st: The brother expected a dry day and thought the umbrella was silly.
The opposite happened: rain came, and he needed the umbrella himself.
An outcome opposite to what was expected is situational irony.
ex.a: Situational irony

topics.rl: Cartoons in newspapers and comedy shows often use irony, for example a 'No Honking' board on a road where everyone keeps honking.

topics.ch: A Letter to God (poems: Dust of Snow, Fire and Ice)
topics.t: Frost poems: symbols, mood and rhyme
topics.h: Can a single bird change your whole day? Robert Frost thought so.
p: 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice' are both by Robert Frost, an American poet.
In 'Dust of Snow', a tiny moment in nature (a crow shaking snow onto the poet) lifts his gloomy mood. The crow and hemlock, usually linked with gloom, bring a change for the better.
In 'Fire and Ice', fire stands for desire and ice stands for hatred; either could destroy the world.
A symbol is an object that stands for an idea beyond itself.
Rhyme scheme: give the same letter to lines whose last words rhyme (a, b, c ...).

ex.q: Poem: A koel called from the neem tree, / Just when my sums went wrong; / My frown slipped off, I don't know how— / The day was saved by song. What is the rhyme scheme?
st: Last words: tree, wrong, how, song.
tree = a, wrong = b, how = c (new sound), song rhymes with wrong = b.
ex.a: abcb

topics.rl: A cup of chai in the rain or a friend's joke can change a bad mood. Poets notice such small moments and turn them into poems.

topics.ch: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom (poem: A Tiger in the Zoo)
topics.t: Apartheid and freedom: tenses
topics.h: Imagine being told which bench, bus or school you may use because of the colour of your skin. That was life under apartheid.
p: 'Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom' is from Mandela's autobiography; it describes his swearing-in as South Africa's first Black President on 10 May 1994.
Apartheid was South Africa's system of racial separation and discrimination; the word means 'apartness'.
Mandela spent 27 years in prison before his release in 1990; for him, freedom meant freeing both the oppressed and the oppressor.
Simple past for a finished action at a stated time: 'He became President in 1994.'

Present perfect for a past action linked to now, often with since/for/already: 'South Africa has changed since 1994.' Past perfect for the earlier of two past actions: 'He had spent 27 years in prison before he was freed.'

ex.q: Fill in: 'By 1994, apartheid ___ (end), and Mandela ___ (become) President.'
st: Two past actions: apartheid ending came first, then Mandela became President.
The earlier action takes the past perfect: had ended.
The later action, at a known past time, takes the simple past: became.
ex.a: By 1994, apartheid had ended, and Mandela became President.

topics.rl: India too fought for freedom and wrote equality into its Constitution. Mandela admired Mahatma Gandhi, who began his struggle against racial injustice in South Africa.

topics.ch: Nelson Mandela: Long Walk to Freedom (poem: A Tiger in the Zoo)
topics.t: Captivity vs freedom: poetic devices
topics.h: A tiger that should rule a jungle paces a few steps of concrete, up and down. Can a poem make us feel its anger?
p: 'A Tiger in the Zoo' by Leslie Norris contrasts a tiger's angry, helpless life in a cage with the free life it should have in the forest.
Contrast places two opposite ideas side by side (cage vs jungle) to make both sharper.
Imagery is language that creates pictures, sounds or feelings in the reader's mind.
Alliteration repeats the same first consonant sound in nearby words: 'guava groves'.
Enjambment is when a sentence runs on into the next line without a pause.

ex.q: Poem: The parakeet in the iron cage / Repeats the words we say; / But in his dreams the guava groves / Of Nashik call him away. Which device is in 'guava groves', and what contrast does the poem make?
st: 'guava groves' repeats the 'g' sound at the start of words, which is alliteration.
The bird is in an 'iron cage' but dreams of open guava groves.
So the poem sets captivity against freedom.
ex.a: Alliteration; the contrast is between the cage (captivity) and the guava groves (freedom).

topics.rl: Wildlife reserves like Jim Corbett and Kaziranga try to protect animals in their natural homes so they can live freely.

topics.ch: Two Stories about Flying (poems: How to Tell Wild Animals, The Ball Poem)
topics.t: Overcoming fear: reported speech (statements)
topics.h: Every expert swimmer, flyer and speaker was once a beginner with shaking knees.
p: 'His First Flight' tells of a young seagull too afraid to fly; hunger finally pushes him off the ledge, and he discovers he can fly.
Reported (indirect) speech tells what someone said without quoting the exact words: He said that ...
When the reporting verb is in the past (said, told), tenses move one step back: is → was, can → could, will → would, has done → had done.
Pronouns change to fit the speaker: 'I' may become he or she.
Words of time and place change: now → then, today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, here → there, this → that.

ex.q: Passage: Tara stood at the edge of the diving board in Pune. 'I can't do it,' she whispered. Her coach, Mr Rao, said, 'You can. I will be right here.' She shut her eyes, jumped, and came up laughing. Report Tara's words: 'I can't do it.'
st: The reporting verb 'whispered' is in the past, so 'can't' becomes 'couldn't'.
'I' refers to Tara, so it becomes 'she'.
Add 'that' after the reporting verb.
ex.a: Tara whispered that she couldn't do it.

topics.rl: News reports use reported speech all the time: 'The coach said that the team was ready.'

topics.ch: Two Stories about Flying (poems: How to Tell Wild Animals, The Ball Poem)
topics.t: Mystery: modals of deduction
topics.h: A plane appears out of a storm, guides a lost pilot home, and then the control tower says no such plane was ever there.
p: 'The Black Aeroplane' is a mystery: a pilot lost in a storm follows a strange black aeroplane to safety, yet the control tower says no other plane was flying.
A mystery gives clues but leaves some questions unanswered, so readers keep guessing.
Modals of deduction show how sure we are: must = almost certain; can't = certain it is not true; may/might/could = possible.
For the past, add 'have' + past participle: 'Someone must have entered.' 'He can't have left.'
Other modals: should (advice), would (polite request), need not/needn't (no necessity).

ex.q: Passage: At midnight, a soft tune drifted from the locked music room of the old Shimla guest house. In the morning, the caretaker, who kept the only key, found fresh rose petals on the piano keys. Using a modal, what can you say about the petals?
st: The petals were fresh in the morning, so they were placed during the night.
Only the caretaker had the key; nobody else could easily enter.
We are almost sure someone was inside, though not who: use 'must have' for strong certainty.
ex.a: Someone must have been in the music room last night.

topics.rl: Detectives, doctors and even weather forecasters use deduction: 'It might rain', 'He must have the flu', 'The thief can't have gone far.'

topics.ch: Two Stories about Flying (poems: How to Tell Wild Animals, The Ball Poem)
topics.t: Loss and growing up: tone in poems
topics.h: Losing a favourite thing hurts. But what if that hurt is also a lesson?
p: 'The Ball Poem' by John Berryman shows a boy who loses his ball and, for the first time, learns what loss means.
The poet does not buy him another ball, because he wants the boy to learn to bear loss himself; that is part of growing up and taking responsibility.
'How to Tell Wild Animals' by Carolyn Wells is a humorous poem that 'teaches' readers to identify animals in a funny, exaggerated way.
Tone is the writer's attitude shown through words: humorous, serious, sad, hopeful, angry.
The same subject can have different tones: the loss of a ball is serious in Berryman; danger from wild animals is funny in Wells.

ex.q: Poem: My kite snapped free above the Jaipur roofs / And drifted past the sun; / I cried, then learnt that some things go— / And growing up's begun. What is the tone of the last line, and what has the speaker learnt?
st: The speaker first cries, so there is sadness.
Then the speaker 'learnt that some things go', which is acceptance.
'Growing up's begun' sounds calm and hopeful.
ex.a: The tone becomes accepting and hopeful; the speaker has learnt that some losses are part of growing up.

topics.rl: Moving to a new city, a friend changing schools or a broken toy all teach us to accept loss and carry on.

topics.ch: From the Diary of Anne Frank (poem: Amanda!)
topics.t: Diary writing
topics.h: A diary is the one friend who listens to everything and never interrupts.
p: 'From the Diary of Anne Frank' comes from the diary of a Jewish girl who got it on her 13th birthday in 1942 and named it Kitty.
She felt she had no true friend to confide in, so the diary became that friend. In school her teacher Mr Keesing gave her extra essays for talking too much in class.
Diary format: date, day and time at the top; 'Dear Diary' (optional); body; your name at the end.
A diary is personal and informal, written in the first person (I, me, my).
Write what happened (mostly past tense) AND how you felt about it.

ex.q: Diary: Monday, 3 March, 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today Miss Iyer made me read my poem aloud. My voice shook at first, but the whole class clapped! I might write another one tonight. — Pihu What two things does a good diary entry like this contain?
st: Events: Pihu read her poem aloud and the class clapped.
Feelings: her voice shook (nervous), then 'clapped!' shows joy.
Format: date, day, time, 'Dear Diary', name at the end.
ex.a: What happened (events) and how the writer felt (feelings), in the proper diary format.

topics.rl: Many people keep a journal or gratitude diary; even a scientist's lab notebook and a ship captain's logbook are kinds of diaries.

topics.ch: From the Diary of Anne Frank (poem: Amanda!)
topics.t: WWII and reported questions
topics.h: A small notebook hidden in an attic became one of the most-read books in the world.
p: The Second World War lasted from 1939 to 1945.
During the war, Jews were persecuted by the Nazis. Anne's family, who lived in Amsterdam, went into hiding in a secret part of a building from 1942 to 1944.
Anne did not survive the war. Her father, Otto Frank, published her diary, which has been translated into many languages.
Reporting yes/no questions: use 'asked + if/whether' and change to statement order: He asked, 'Are you ready?' → He asked if I was ready.
Reporting wh-questions: keep the wh-word and use statement order, no question mark: She asked, 'Where do you live?' → She asked me where I lived.

ex.q: Report this: Mr Keesing asked Anne, 'Why are you talking again?'
st: It is a wh-question, so keep 'why'.
Use statement order: subject before verb ('she was talking').
Shift the tense back: are → was; 'you' becomes 'she'; drop the question mark.
ex.a: Mr Keesing asked Anne why she was talking again.

topics.rl: Interviewers and reporters often write questions this way: 'The reporter asked the minister when the bridge would open.'

topics.ch: From the Diary of Anne Frank (poem: Amanda!)
topics.t: Childhood freedom: sentence types
topics.h: 'Do this! Don't do that!' Ever wished you could fly away from all the instructions?
p: 'Amanda!' by Robin Klein shows a girl who is given non-stop instructions; she escapes in her imagination into daydreams of freedom, such as being a mermaid or Rapunzel.
The poem's message: children need some freedom and space, not constant nagging.
Sentence types: declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request), exclamatory (strong feeling).
Imperative sentences usually begin with a verb and have an understood 'you': 'Sit straight!', 'Don't shout.'
In poems like this, lines in brackets can show a child's inner thoughts.

ex.q: Poem: Sit straight, Ishaan! Don't swing your feet! / (I'm a falcon over Ladakh's peaks.) / Finish your milk and comb your hair! / (Up here there's only sky and air.) What do the lines in brackets show?
st: The other lines are commands: Sit straight! Finish your milk!
The bracketed lines describe flying over Ladakh, which Ishaan is not really doing.
So they are his daydreams, his escape from the instructions.
ex.a: They show Ishaan's imagination: he daydreams of being free while being given orders.

topics.rl: Hobbies, outdoor play and free time help children relax and think creatively.

topics.t: Goa's bakers: used to and would
topics.h: In old Goa, you could tell the time of morning by the baker's call outside your gate!
p: 'Glimpses of India' has three travel pieces: a baker from Goa, a visit to Coorg, and tea from Assam.
In Goa, traditional bakers are called paders. The baking tradition goes back to the days of Portuguese rule, and bread is part of festivals and weddings.
The Goa piece is nostalgic: it looks back fondly at the past.
'Used to' + verb shows a past habit or state that is no longer true: 'He used to come every day.'
'Would' + verb can also show a repeated past action (not a past state): 'We would wait at the gate.' In questions and negatives, write 'use to': 'Did you use to ...?'

ex.q: Passage: When Nani was a girl in Margao, the baker used to come every morning with a basket of warm bread on his head. The children would rush to the gate the moment they heard his horn, hoping for a sweet bun. Which phrases show past habits, and why?
st: 'used to come every morning' shows something that happened regularly in the past.
'would rush to the gate' also shows a repeated past action.
Both suggest it does not happen in the same way now.
ex.a: 'used to come' and 'would rush'; both describe repeated actions in the past.

topics.rl: Grandparents often begin stories with 'We used to ...'. Ask yours what they used to eat or play as children!

topics.t: Coorg and Assam: degrees of comparison
topics.h: One region smells of coffee, the other of tea. Can you guess which is which?
p: Coorg (Kodagu) is a hilly district of Karnataka, famous for coffee estates, rainforests and its brave Kodava people.
The River Kaveri rises in the hills of Coorg, and the area is popular for adventure sports like river rafting.
Assam is India's largest tea-producing state. In 'Tea from Assam', two friends, Pranjol and Rajvir, travel to a tea garden and talk about legends of how tea was discovered.
Adjectives have three degrees: positive (tall), comparative for two things (taller, more beautiful), superlative for three or more (tallest, most beautiful).
Some are irregular: good-better-best, bad-worse-worst, many/much-more-most, little-less-least.

ex.q: Complete: 'Coorg's hills are ___ (green) than the plains, and the coffee there is the ___ (good) I have tasted.'
st: Two things are compared in the first part, so use the comparative: greener.
The second part compares with everything tasted: superlative.
'Good' is irregular: good-better-best.
ex.a: greener; best

topics.rl: Travel websites and brochures constantly compare: 'the coolest hill station', 'cheaper than flying'.

topics.t: Writing a travel description; 'The Trees'
topics.h: A good travel description lets your reader smell the spices without leaving the sofa.
p: A travel description says where you went and how, then paints the place with details, and ends with your overall impression.
Use sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste and touch.
Order of adjectives: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose: 'a lovely little old red Kashmiri shawl'.
'The Trees' by Adrienne Rich shows trees moving out of a house back into the forest, suggesting that living things long to be free.
Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things: 'the trees stretch their roots', 'the wind whispered'.

ex.q: Passage: We reached Munnar by noon. Mist curled over the rolling green tea hills, and the air smelled of cardamom. A tiny old wooden stall sold hot banana fritters that crackled in the pan. Which senses does this description use?
st: 'Mist curled over rolling green tea hills' is what we see: sight.
'smelled of cardamom' is smell.
'crackled in the pan' is sound, and 'hot fritters' suggests taste and touch.
ex.a: Sight, smell, sound, and also taste/touch through 'hot banana fritters'.

topics.rl: Travel bloggers and tourism boards, like those for Kerala or Meghalaya, use sensory details to attract visitors.

topics.t: A pet otter: subject-verb agreement
topics.h: Imagine a pet that turns your bathtub into a water park every single day!
p: In 'Mijbil the Otter', Gavin Maxwell brings home an otter from Iraq and names him Mijbil (Mij).
Mij turned out to be of a kind of otter not known to science before, so it was named after Maxwell: Maxwell's otter.
Subject-verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb (The otter swims); a plural subject takes a plural verb (Otters swim).
Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb. With 'each', 'every', 'either of', 'neither of' and 'one of the ...', use a singular verb.
With 'either...or' or 'neither...nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject. With 'along with' or 'as well as', it agrees with the first subject.

ex.q: Passage: Our puppy, Laddoo, and our old cat, Mishri, share the sunny corner of the verandah. Neither of them likes the noisy mixer. Every morning, the pair races to the kitchen when the milk boils. Why does the passage say 'Neither of them likes', not 'like'?
st: The subject is 'Neither of them'.
'Neither' means not this one and not that one, taken one at a time.
So it is treated as singular and takes 'likes'.
ex.a: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb, so 'likes' is correct.

topics.rl: Board exam gap-filling and editing questions often test agreement: 'Each of the students has a book.'

topics.t: Animal behaviour: verbs and adverbs
topics.h: Otters slide, splash, juggle and even sulk. Watching them is like watching a comedy show!
p: Mij loved water: he played and splashed in the bath, and was full of playful energy.
He travelled to London by plane, packed in a box, and later made the flat his playground.
Strong, precise verbs describe behaviour vividly: a snake slithers, a duck waddles, a tiger prowls, a mouse scurries.
Adverbs tell how an action is done: The otter swam gracefully. Many are formed by adding -ly to an adjective (graceful → gracefully).
Careful observers note what an animal does, when and how often, without exaggerating.

ex.q: Passage: The otter on the Chambal bank slid down the mud, splashed into the river, and bobbed up with a fish, chirping happily. Then it rolled over and over on the warm sand. Which words show that the otter is playful and happy?
st: 'slid down the mud' and 'rolled over and over' are play actions.
'splashed' and 'bobbed up' show it enjoying the water.
'chirping happily': the adverb 'happily' tells us its mood.
ex.a: slid, splashed, rolled over and over, and 'chirping happily'.

topics.rl: Smooth-coated otters live in Indian rivers like the Chambal. Wildlife scientists record their behaviour to protect them.

topics.t: Metaphor: 'Fog' and beyond
topics.h: What if fog were a cat that tiptoes into the city and then quietly walks away?
p: 'Fog' by Carl Sandburg compares the fog to a cat: it arrives silently, sits and watches the city, then moves on.
A metaphor says one thing IS another, without 'like' or 'as': 'The classroom was a zoo.'
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as': 'He runs like a cheetah.'
An extended metaphor carries one comparison through many lines, as with the fog and the cat.
Personification gives human qualities to non-human things; metaphors often work alongside it.

ex.q: Poem: Evening is a grey heron / Standing still on one leg; / It folds the river in its wings / And flies off into the night. What is evening compared to, and is it a simile or a metaphor?
st: Evening is directly called 'a grey heron'.
There is no 'like' or 'as'.
The comparison continues: it stands, folds its wings and flies off, so it is extended.
ex.a: Evening is compared to a grey heron; it is an (extended) metaphor.

topics.rl: We use metaphors every day: 'Mumbai never sleeps', 'my brother is a couch potato', 'time is money'.

topics.ch: Madam Rides the Bus (poem: The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
topics.t: A child's curiosity: reporting commands and requests
topics.h: What is so exciting about a bus ride? Ask any child who has watched the world rush past the window!
p: In 'Madam Rides the Bus' by Vallikkannan, a curious village girl, Valli, longs to ride the bus to town. She saves her coins carefully and makes the trip on her own.
Her curiosity, careful planning and confidence make her a lively young 'madam'. The journey also teaches her something about life.
Reported commands and requests use: told/ordered/requested/advised/warned + person + to + verb.
Negative commands use 'not to': 'Don't lean out' → He warned me not to lean out.
'Please' is dropped; its meaning goes into the verb 'requested'.

ex.q: Passage: Chintu pressed his nose to the bus window in Chennai. 'Uncle, please open the window wider,' he said to the conductor. 'Don't lean out,' the conductor warned, smiling. Report what Chintu said to the conductor.
st: It is a polite request ('please'), so use 'requested'.
Drop 'please' and use 'to' + verb: to open.
'Uncle' is a form of address and is dropped; 'the conductor' becomes the object.
ex.a: Chintu requested the conductor to open the window wider.

topics.rl: Signboards and instructions are commands in short form: 'Do not lean out of the window', 'Please stand in a queue.'

topics.ch: Madam Rides the Bus (poem: The Tale of Custard the Dragon)
topics.t: A humorous ballad: Custard the Dragon
topics.h: A dragon who is scared of everything? That sounds like the funniest hero ever!
p: 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon' by Ogden Nash is a humorous ballad about Belinda and her pets: Ink the kitten, Blink the mouse, Mustard the dog, and Custard, a 'cowardly' dragon.
Everyone teases Custard for being a coward, but when a pirate arrives, he is the one who fights while the others hide: a funny twist that shows true courage.
A ballad is a poem that tells a story, usually in short stanzas with a regular rhyme and rhythm, often with repetition.
This ballad rhymes in couplets: aabb.
Humour comes from exaggeration, made-up words, funny names and the surprise ending.

ex.q: Ballad: In Madurai lived a girl named Meera, / With a parrot called Pista and a goat called Heera, / And a timid old buffalo, slow as a snail, / Who once chased a thief all the way to the jail! Find the rhyme scheme and the funny twist.
st: Meera/Heera rhyme: a a.
snail/jail rhyme: b b.
The twist: a 'timid', snail-slow buffalo is the one who chases a thief.
ex.a: The rhyme scheme is aabb; the humour is that the timid, slow buffalo turns out to be the hero.

topics.rl: Folk songs and storytelling traditions across India, from Rajasthan to Assam, tell tales in rhyming verse, much like ballads.

topics.ch: The Sermon at Benares (poem: For Anne Gregory)
topics.t: Coping with grief: connectors
topics.h: A mother looks for a cure for her sorrow and is asked for something very simple: a few mustard seeds. Why?
p: 'The Sermon at Benares' tells how Gautama Buddha helped Kisa Gotami, a mother grieving for her son.
He asked her to bring mustard seed from a house where no one had ever died. She found no such house and understood that death comes to every family.
The teaching: grief is natural, but endless sorrow brings only more pain; understanding that loss is shared by all can bring peace.
Connectors join ideas: contrast (although, but, however), reason (because, since, as), result (so, therefore), addition (and, moreover).
'However' and 'therefore' usually link two sentences: 'It rained. However, the fair went on.'

ex.q: Passage: When Arjun's grandfather passed away, Arjun shut himself in his room. His aunt sat beside him and said gently, 'Every family we know has lost someone. Grief shared is grief halved.' Slowly, Arjun opened the window. What did the aunt mean by 'Grief shared is grief halved'?
st: She reminds Arjun that every family has lost someone.
So he is not alone in his sorrow.
Talking about it with others makes the pain lighter, just as Kisa Gotami found that loss is common to all.
ex.a: Sharing sorrow with others makes it easier to bear.

topics.rl: Families across India come together after a loss to support each other; comfort from others helps people heal.

topics.ch: The Sermon at Benares (poem: For Anne Gregory)
topics.t: Inner vs outer beauty: opposites with prefixes
topics.h: Would you rather be liked for your hair or for your heart?
p: 'For Anne Gregory' is by the Irish poet W.B. Yeats. A young woman wants to be loved for herself, not for her beautiful yellow hair.
The older speaker replies that people are usually attracted first by outer looks; the poem contrasts outer beauty with inner worth.
Inner beauty: kindness, honesty, courage. Outer beauty: looks, hair, clothes.
Many opposites are formed with prefixes: un- (unkind), in- (invisible), im- before p/m (impossible, immature), il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular), dis- (dishonest).
Superficial means 'only on the surface', which is the opposite of looking at inner qualities.

ex.q: Poem: 'Don't praise my curls,' my sister said, / 'Praise the kindness that I do.' / Dadi laughed, 'Child, most eyes will see / Your curls before they look at you.' What does the sister want, and what does Dadi say about the world?
st: The sister wants her kindness praised, not her curls: inner beauty.
Dadi says most people notice curls (outer beauty) first.
So the poem contrasts inner and outer beauty.
ex.a: The sister wants to be valued for her kindness; Dadi says people usually notice looks first.

topics.rl: Long after school photos fade, friends remember who was kind, honest and helpful. Character outlasts looks.

topics.t: A one-act comic play: how plays work
topics.h: A man comes to propose marriage, but ends up fighting about a meadow and a dog. Only on stage!
p: 'The Proposal' by Anton Chekhov is a one-act comic play: Lomov visits his neighbour Chubukov to propose to his daughter Natalya.
Before he can propose, Lomov and Natalya quarrel about the Oxen Meadows, and later about whose dog is better. They get engaged, but keep quarrelling.
A one-act play is short, has one act, few characters and usually one setting.
A play is told through dialogue; stage directions (often in brackets or italics) tell actors how to move and speak.
A farce is a comedy built on exaggerated characters and silly situations.

ex.q: Scene: RAHUL (nervously): Uncle, I have come to ask... to ask... / MR VERMA (smiling): Speak up, beta! / RAHUL (clutching his chest): My heart is pounding! What do the words in brackets do?
st: '(nervously)', '(smiling)', '(clutching his chest)' are not spoken aloud.
They tell the actor how to speak or what to do.
So they are stage directions.
ex.a: They are stage directions: they show how the characters speak and act.

topics.rl: School annual-day plays, street plays (nukkad natak) and TV sitcoms all use dialogue and stage directions.

topics.t: Chekhov and comic characters: describing traits
topics.h: A man who claims his heart is pounding and his leg is numb, every few minutes! Chekhov makes it hilarious.
p: Anton Chekhov (1860-1904) was a Russian writer of plays and short stories, and also a doctor.
In 'The Proposal', Lomov keeps complaining about his health: palpitations, a numb leg. He worries too much about illness.
The humour comes from exaggeration and irony: people meant to be planning a marriage quarrel over trifles.
Character-trait words: quarrelsome (likes to argue), hypochondriac (worries too much about health), irritable (easily annoyed), impulsive (acts without thinking).
Many adjectives come from nouns with suffixes: quarrel → quarrelsome, nerve → nervous, humour → humorous, anger → angry.

ex.q: In the play, Lomov complains of palpitations and a numb foot every time Natalya disagrees with him about a small matter. What trait does this show, and why is it funny?
st: He reacts to a small argument as if he is seriously ill.
That shows he worries too much about his health: a hypochondriac.
The gap between the tiny cause and his huge reaction is exaggeration, which makes us laugh.
ex.a: He is a hypochondriac; his huge reaction to a small quarrel is comic exaggeration.

topics.rl: Comedians often exaggerate everyday habits, such as an uncle who checks the gas knob ten times before leaving.

topics.t: A pampered dog: the passive voice
topics.h: Cream cakes, chocolates and extra treats every day: is that love or trouble for a little dog?
p: 'A Triumph of Surgery' by James Herriot, a vet, tells of Tricki Woo, a pet dog over-fed and spoiled by his rich owner, Mrs Pumphrey.
Tricki becomes ill and lazy. The vet takes him to his surgery, gives him no food for two days, and lets him play and run with the other dogs. Tricki recovers fully.
Passive voice puts the receiver of the action first: 'Tricki was fed cream cakes.' Form: be + past participle.
The doer can be added with 'by', or left out when it is unknown or unimportant: 'The dog was taken to the surgery.'
Keep the tense the same: is fed (present), was fed (past), has been fed (present perfect), will be fed (future).

ex.q: Passage: Bruno, a spoilt beagle in Bandra, was given jalebis and ice cream every day. Soon he was too fat to climb the stairs. He was taken to the vet, was put on a strict diet, and was made to run in the park. Why does the writer use the passive voice here?
st: The sentences focus on what happened TO Bruno: was given, was taken, was put, was made.
Who did it (owner, vet) is less important than Bruno's story.
So the passive keeps Bruno as the subject of every sentence.
ex.a: To keep the focus on Bruno, the one receiving the actions, rather than on who did them.

topics.rl: Notices and news reports use the passive: 'The road will be closed on Sunday', 'Two tigers were spotted in Ranthambore.'

topics.t: Humour in the story: irony and idioms
topics.h: A dog is 'cured by surgery' without a single cut. How is that a triumph?
p: The title 'A Triumph of Surgery' is ironic: no operation was done; simple diet and exercise cured Tricki.
The story is told by the vet, James Herriot, with gentle humour about Mrs Pumphrey's over-indulgence.
Humour devices: irony (opposite of what is expected), hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration), and funny contrasts.
Idioms are phrases whose meaning differs from the separate words: 'in the pink of health' = very healthy.
Use idioms sparingly and correctly in writing; they make it lively but must fit the context.

ex.q: Mrs Kapoor feeds her pug so many laddoos that 'they could feed a whole wedding'. Which humour device is this?
st: No one could really feed a whole wedding with one pug's laddoos.
The writer exaggerates on purpose to make us laugh.
Deliberate exaggeration is hyperbole.
ex.a: Hyperbole (deliberate exaggeration).

topics.rl: Cartoonists like R.K. Laxman used gentle exaggeration and irony to make readers smile about everyday life.

topics.t: Trust and reform: narrative tenses
topics.h: A thief steals from the only person who ever trusted him, then something stops him at the railway station.
p: 'The Thief's Story' by Ruskin Bond is narrated by Hari Singh, a young thief who befriends Anil, a writer.
Anil gives him work and teaches him to read and write. Hari steals Anil's money but returns, realising that learning and Anil's trust are worth far more.
Anil quietly knows but says nothing; his trust helps Hari reform (change for the better).
Stories use narrative tenses: simple past for main events (he crept), past continuous for background actions (Anil was sleeping), past perfect for earlier events (he had decided).
'While' usually takes past continuous; 'when' often introduces a simple past action that interrupts.

ex.q: Passage: While Anil was sleeping, Hari crept to the mattress. He had already decided to run away. But at the station, as the train was leaving, he remembered Anil's kindness and turned back. Name the tense of each underlined idea: 'was sleeping', 'had decided', 'turned back'.
st: 'was sleeping' is background going on at the time: past continuous.
'had decided' happened before he crept: past perfect.
'turned back' is a main event: simple past.
ex.a: was sleeping = past continuous; had decided = past perfect; turned back = simple past.

topics.rl: When you tell a friend what happened at a cricket match, you naturally mix these tenses: 'We were batting when it started to rain.'

topics.t: Writing a character sketch: words for change
topics.h: A thief who becomes a student. What changed inside him, and how do we describe it?
p: A character sketch describes a person's traits, each supported by evidence from the story.
Structure: introduction (who the person is), 2-3 traits with examples, any change in the character, and a closing line.
Hari changes from a thief who cheats to a young man who values education and trust; Anil is kind and trusting.
Words for inner change: conscience (inner sense of right and wrong), remorse (deep regret), reform (change for the better), gratitude (thankfulness).
Word families: trust (noun/verb), trusting, trustworthy, distrust.

ex.q: Write one trait of Anil with evidence.
st: Pick a trait: trusting.
Find what he does: he knows Hari took the money, yet says nothing and keeps teaching him.
Join trait + evidence in one sentence.
ex.a: Anil is trusting: even after Hari takes his money, he says nothing and carries on teaching him.

topics.rl: Teachers, coaches and employers write similar sketches in reports and references: 'Riya is responsible: she never misses a deadline.'

topics.t: A spy story: clues and conditionals
topics.h: A spy who is fat, ordinary-looking and carries no gadgets. Can he still win?
p: 'The Midnight Visitor' by Robert Arthur features Ausable, a secret agent who looks nothing like the glamorous spies of films; a young writer, Fowler, is disappointed by him.
In Ausable's room they find Max, a rival agent with a pistol, who has come for an important secret paper.
Spy stories have secret missions, suspense, clues and a twist at the end.
Conditionals: first conditional for a real possibility (If + present, will + verb): 'If the police come, they will search the room.'
Second conditional for an imaginary situation (If + past, would + verb): 'If I were a spy, I would carry a camera.' Use 'were' for all persons in formal English.

ex.q: Passage: Agent Kavya noticed that the 'courier' wore shiny, spotless shoes on a muddy Cherrapunji morning. She smiled, handed him an empty envelope, and quietly alerted her team. What clue gave the 'courier' away?
st: The morning was muddy, so anyone walking outside would have muddy shoes.
His shoes were shiny and spotless.
So he was probably not who he claimed to be.
ex.a: His spotless shoes on a muddy morning showed he was not a real courier.

topics.rl: Detective and spy stories, from Byomkesh Bakshi to Feluda, keep readers hooked by hiding clues in plain sight.

topics.t: Quick thinking: sequence words and story writing
topics.h: One made-up balcony, one knock at the door, and a dangerous man is gone. That's thinking fast!
p: Ausable stays calm in danger. He invents a balcony below his window and tells Max the police are about to come.
When there is a knock, Max panics and climbs out onto the 'balcony', which does not exist. The knock was only a waiter bringing drinks Ausable had ordered.
Presence of mind means thinking calmly and quickly in an emergency; Ausable uses wit, not weapons.
Sequence words organise a story: first, then, next, after that, suddenly (for surprise), finally.
A good short story has a clear beginning, a problem, a turning point and an ending.

ex.q: Put in sequence words: '___ the lights went out. ___ we heard footsteps. ___ the door creaked open. ___ it was only Dadi with a candle!'
st: The opening event comes first: 'First,'.
The next event: 'Then,'.
The unexpected moment: 'Suddenly,'.
The ending: 'Finally,'.
ex.a: First, Then, Suddenly, Finally.

topics.rl: In a real emergency, like a power cut in a lift, staying calm and thinking clearly is the best help.

topics.t: Irony in 'A Question of Trust': proverbs
topics.h: A master thief who plans everything perfectly is fooled in five minutes by a charming stranger!
p: 'A Question of Trust' by Victor Canning is about Horace Danby, a respected lock-maker who secretly robs one safe a year to buy rare books.
While robbing a house, he meets a young woman who pretends to be the lady of the house. She persuades him to open the safe for her and leaves with the jewels.
Horace had taken off his gloves, so his fingerprints are on the safe. He is arrested for a theft he was tricked into, and nobody believes his story.
The irony: a clever thief is himself cheated by another thief; the careful planner who left nothing to chance ends up trusting the wrong person.
Proverbs sum up such lessons: 'As you sow, so shall you reap' means we face the results of our own actions.

ex.q: Passage: Mr Bose, who sells 'unbreakable' anti-theft locks in Kolkata, returned from his shop one evening to find that his own scooter had been stolen from outside his house. Why is this situation ironic?
st: Mr Bose sells locks that are supposed to stop theft.
Yet his own scooter is stolen.
The outcome is the opposite of what we would expect for him, so it is situational irony.
ex.a: It is situational irony: a seller of anti-theft locks becomes a victim of theft himself.

topics.rl: News sometimes reports ironic events, like a 'No Parking' board being towed away, and readers enjoy the twist.

topics.t: Crime words and reporting a crime
topics.h: Burglar, alibi, accomplice: every detective and reporter needs these words!
p: Crime vocabulary: theft (stealing), burglary (breaking into a building to steal), forgery (making fakes), accomplice (helper in a crime), suspect (person thought guilty), alibi (proof you were elsewhere), witness (person who saw it).
A news report starts with a short headline and a dateline (place and date).
The first paragraph (the lead) answers the 5Ws and 1H: who, what, when, where, why, how.
News reports are factual and use the third person; the passive voice is common ('was arrested').
Crime stories in literature often end with justice, reminding readers that wrongdoing has consequences.

ex.q: News: Pune, 12 March: A locksmith was arrested on Tuesday after police found his fingerprints on a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow. Jewellery worth lakhs is missing. Find who, what, when and where.
st: Who: a locksmith.
What: was arrested; jewellery missing.
When: Tuesday (dateline 12 March).
Where: a bungalow in Koregaon Park, Pune.
ex.a: Who: a locksmith; what: arrested over missing jewellery; when: Tuesday; where: Koregaon Park, Pune.

topics.rl: Newspapers like those you see at home follow this format every day: headline, dateline, then the key facts first.

topics.t: The invisible man: words about seeing
topics.h: Imagine footprints appearing on a London street with nobody standing in them!
p: 'Footprints without Feet' by H.G. Wells is about Griffin, a brilliant scientist who makes his body invisible by swallowing certain rare drugs.
Two boys in London are amazed to see fresh muddy footprints appear on the steps with no one there.
Griffin finds being invisible far from easy: he must stay unclothed to be unseen, so he feels cold and has to find clothes and shelter. He soon turns to wrongdoing.
Vocabulary: transparent (clearly see-through), translucent (lets some light through, not clearly), opaque (lets no light through), invisible (cannot be seen).
The prefix in- often means 'not': invisible, incorrect, incomplete.

ex.q: Passage: The new glass door at the mall was so clean and transparent that Bunty walked straight into it. He rubbed his nose while his sister giggled behind him. Why did Bunty walk into the door?
st: The door was clean glass.
It was transparent, so light passed through it and he could see straight through.
He did not notice it was there.
ex.a: The door was so transparent that he did not see it.

topics.rl: Science-fiction ideas inspire real research, such as 'invisibility cloaks' that bend light in labs, though nothing like Griffin's has been made.

topics.t: Science and ethics: letter to the editor
topics.h: If you could become invisible, would you use it for good? Griffin's answer is a warning.
p: Griffin misuses his discovery: instead of sharing it for good, he uses invisibility to steal and frighten people.
The story raises a question of ethics (moral principles of right and wrong): a great discovery needs responsibility.

A letter to the editor gives your views on a public issue. Format: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, complimentary close (Yours faithfully), signature and name.
The body: introduce the issue, give reasons and examples, suggest solutions, and close politely.
Keep the tone formal, polite and to the point; avoid slang and personal attacks.

ex.q: Write a suitable subject line for a letter to the editor about people flying drones over a crowded festival ground.
st: A subject line is short and states the issue clearly.
Name the problem: unsafe drone flying.
Name the place or event: crowded festival grounds.
ex.a: Subject: Unsafe flying of drones over crowded festival grounds

topics.rl: Letters to the editor in newspapers let citizens raise issues like noise, traffic, cleanliness or the safe use of technology.

topics.ch: Footprints: The Making of a Scientist
topics.t: Richard Ebright: the making of a scientist
topics.h: A boy who couldn't stop collecting butterflies grew up to study how living cells work.
p: 'The Making of a Scientist' by Robert W. Peterson tells the story of Richard H. Ebright, an American scientist who began by collecting butterflies as a child.
His mother encouraged him strongly; she gave him the book 'The Travels of Monarch X', which led him to tag monarch butterflies for research.
Through school science-fair projects, such as testing whether viceroy butterflies copy monarchs, he learnt to ask questions and test them.
As a college student, he and a friend worked out a theory of how cells read their DNA.
The lesson names three things that make a scientist: a first-rate mind, curiosity, and the will to win for the right reasons.

ex.q: Think it through: Ebright's first science-fair project did not win. What did he learn from that, as a scientist would?
st: Losing showed him that just displaying things was not enough.
He began doing real experiments that test a question.
So failure pushed him to improve instead of giving up.
ex.a: That science means asking a question and testing it with experiments; a setback is a chance to improve.

topics.rl: Indian scientists like C.V. Raman and A.P.J. Abdul Kalam also began with a childhood curiosity about the world around them.

topics.ch: Footprints: The Making of a Scientist
topics.t: Curiosity in numbers: the analytical paragraph
topics.h: Data tells a story too. Can you read it like a scientist?
p: Curious people ask 'why' and 'what if', then look at evidence, often in the form of data.
An analytical paragraph describes data from a chart or table in about 100-150 words.
Structure: introduction (what the data shows), body (main trends with exact figures and comparisons), conclusion (overall picture).
Trend words: rose/increased, fell/decreased, peaked (reached its highest), remained steady, fluctuated (rose and fell), doubled.
Use the past tense for past data, quote figures accurately, and do not add personal opinions not shown by the data.

ex.q: Data: Science club members at Sunrise School: 2021: 20, 2022: 28, 2023: 35, 2024: 33, 2025: 50. Write an opening sentence and one trend sentence.
st: Opening: say what the data is about and the period.
Trend: membership went from 20 to 35 between 2021 and 2023.
Then it fell slightly to 33 before rising to 50 in 2025.
ex.a: The chart shows science club membership at Sunrise School from 2021 to 2025. Membership rose from 20 to 35 by 2023, dipped slightly to 33 in 2024 and peaked at 50 in 2025.

topics.rl: Reports on rainfall, cricket scores, and school results all use analytical writing to explain numbers.

topics.t: Maupassant's twist: relative clauses
topics.h: One borrowed necklace, one lost night, ten hard years, and then a final sentence that changes everything.
p: 'The Necklace' is by Guy de Maupassant, a French writer famous for short stories with surprise (twist) endings.
Matilda Loisel, unhappy with her simple life, borrows a diamond necklace from her rich friend Madame Forestier for a party, and loses it.
The Loisels secretly buy a costly replacement and spend years in hardship repaying the debt. Finally Matilda learns the original necklace was fake.
Relative pronouns join clauses: who (people), which (things), whose (possession), that (people or things in defining clauses).
A non-defining clause adds extra information and is set off by commas: 'Rani, who loved to look rich, ...'. Do not use 'that' in such clauses.

ex.q: Passage: Rani, who loved to look rich, borrowed her cousin's silk sari for a wedding in Lucknow. The sari, which she wore proudly, tore on a nail. She worked for months to buy a new one, only to hear her cousin laugh, 'That was a cheap copy!' Join: 'The cousin laughed. Rani had borrowed the cousin's sari.'
st: The second sentence tells us something the cousin owns: the sari.
Possession is shown with 'whose'.
Put the clause right after 'the cousin'.
ex.a: The cousin whose sari Rani had borrowed laughed.

topics.rl: Twist endings are loved in Indian storytelling too, from Panchatantra-style fables to TV mysteries.

topics.t: Vanity and its cost: abstract nouns
topics.h: Was one evening of looking rich worth ten years of hard work?
p: Matilda's vanity (too much pride in looks and status) makes her borrow the necklace so she can appear rich.
Instead of telling Madame Forestier the truth, the Loisels borrow heavily, buy a replacement and spend 10 years in hard work and poverty to repay the debt.
The lesson: vanity and false pride can be very costly; honesty and contentment could have saved them.
Abstract nouns name qualities and feelings. Many come from adjectives: vain → vanity, proud → pride, humble → humility, generous → generosity, content → contentment.
Opposites: vanity ↔ modesty, pride ↔ humility, greed ↔ contentment.

ex.q: Think it through: What one honest action could have saved the Loisels from years of hardship?
st: They lost a borrowed necklace.
They hid this and bought an expensive replacement.
If they had told Madame Forestier the truth, they would have learnt it was fake.
ex.a: Telling Madame Forestier the truth about losing the necklace.

topics.rl: Social media can tempt people to show off; being content with who we are saves money and stress.

topics.t: Girls' education: formal letter of complaint
topics.h: A girl everyone called 'simpleton' ends the story by speaking up louder than anyone. What changed her?
p: 'Bholi' by K.A. Abbas is about Sulekha, nicknamed Bholi, a girl who was laughed at and ignored at home.
She is sent to school, where a kind teacher encourages her. Education gives her knowledge, courage and self-respect.
In India, the Right to Education Act, 2009, gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6 to 14.
A letter of complaint is a formal letter: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, Sir/Madam, body, Yours faithfully, name.
Body of a complaint: state the problem, give exact details (where, since when, effects), request specific action, and thank the reader.

ex.q: Passage: When Lata joined the village school at nine, she hid behind the last bench. Her teacher, Sunita Ma'am, lent her a picture book every Friday. A year later, Lata read the Republic Day speech aloud to the whole school. What changed Lata, and what does this show about education?
st: At first she hid behind the last bench: she was shy.
Her teacher kept lending her books: encouragement.
A year later she spoke to the whole school: education and a caring teacher built her confidence.
ex.a: Her teacher's encouragement and books; education builds a child's confidence.

topics.rl: Schemes like 'Beti Bachao Beti Padhao' (launched in 2015) encourage families to educate their daughters.

topics.t: Self-confidence: modals of ability, permission and duty
topics.h: 'I can.' 'I may.' 'I must.' Tiny words, but they say a lot about confidence!
p: As a child, Bholi stammered and was mocked, so she hardly spoke.
At school she learns to speak and read. At the end she speaks firmly and decides to teach at the school where she learnt so much.
Modals show ability (can, could), permission (may, can), obligation (must, have to), advice (should) and no necessity (needn't).
'Must' shows strong obligation, often from the speaker; 'have to' often shows a rule from outside: 'We have to wear uniforms.'
'Could' is the past of 'can' for ability: 'At five, I could swim.'

ex.q: Choose modals: 'At first Bholi ___ not speak clearly. Later she ___ speak confidently. Everyone ___ respect her choice.'
st: First blank: past inability: could.
Second: ability she gained: could (or was able to).
Third: a strong duty: must.
ex.a: could; could (was able to); must

topics.rl: Confident speakers say 'I can try' instead of 'I can't'. School debates and assemblies build this skill.

topics.ch: Footprints: The Book That Saved the Earth
topics.t: A science-fiction play: word roots of the future
topics.h: Martians plan to invade Earth, and are stopped by a book of nursery rhymes!
p: 'The Book That Saved the Earth' by Claire Boiko is a science-fiction play introduced by a historian from the 25th century.
From Mars, the proud leader Think-Tank and his apprentice Noodle guide a crew (Captain Omega, Lieutenant Iota and Sergeant Oop) who land on Earth, enter a library and try to understand its books.
Reading a book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes, they take the silly verses as secret warnings, panic and call off the invasion.
Science fiction imagines future science, space travel and other worlds; it often comments on our own world.
Science words often use Greek or Latin roots: tele- (far), micro- (small), astro- (star), bio- (life), -scope (instrument for viewing).

ex.q: Think it through: What do 'telescope' and 'microscope' mean, using their roots?
st: tele- means far; micro- means small.
-scope means an instrument for viewing.
So a telescope views far things and a microscope views very small things.
ex.a: Telescope: an instrument to see distant things; microscope: an instrument to see very small things.

topics.rl: ISRO's missions, like Chandrayaan and Mangalyaan, show how yesterday's science fiction becomes today's science.

topics.ch: Footprints: The Book That Saved the Earth
topics.t: Humour in the play: misunderstandings, puns and homophones
topics.h: A mighty Martian leader frightened by an egg sitting on a wall: comedy at its best!
p: The play's humour comes from misunderstanding: the Martians read simple nursery rhymes as serious codes.
Think-Tank is conceited (too proud of himself) and insults his apprentice Noodle, yet he is the one who is fooled.
Dramatic irony: the audience knows the rhymes are harmless, but the Martians are terrified.
A pun plays on two meanings of a word, or on words that sound alike: 'The book on anti-gravity is impossible to put down.'
Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning: read/reed, their/there, knight/night, write/right.

ex.q: Why is it funny that Think-Tank, who thinks he is brilliant, is scared off by a nursery rhyme?
st: He boasts of his great mind and mocks Noodle.
Yet he cannot understand simple children's verses.
The proud one being fooled by something harmless is ironic and comic.
ex.a: His pride makes the misunderstanding funnier: the 'genius' is beaten by a children's rhyme.

topics.rl: Comedy films and TV shows often use mix-ups and wordplay, like a character mishearing 'desert' as 'dessert'.

qa.q: Passage: After the hailstorm, Hari's cotton field lay flat. His children cried, but Hari looked at the sky and smiled, 'Help will come.' Next morning he borrowed seeds and sowed again. What did Hari do the next morning?
qa.a: He borrowed seeds and sowed again.
qa.e: The last line says he borrowed seeds and sowed again.

qa.q: Passage: After the hailstorm, Hari's cotton field lay flat. His children cried, but Hari looked at the sky and smiled, 'Help will come.' Next morning he borrowed seeds and sowed again. Which word best describes Hari?
qa.e: He smiles, says help will come and starts sowing again, so he is hopeful.

qa.q: In 'A Letter to God', what ruins the farmer's crop?
qa.e: Rain first turns into a heavy hailstorm that destroys the crop.

qa.q: To whom does the farmer in 'A Letter to God' write his letter?
qa.e: His faith makes him write directly to God for money to sow again.

qa.q: What does the word 'faith' mean?
qa.e: Faith is complete trust or belief in someone or something.

qa.q: Choose the determiner: 'We had ___ rain this monsoon, so the crops dried up.'
qa.e: Rain is uncountable, and 'little' means hardly any, which explains why crops dried up.

qa.q: Which sentence uses a determiner correctly?
qa.a: He has many friends in the village.
qa.e: 'Friends' is countable plural, so 'many' is correct.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'hopeful'?
qa.e: Despairing means having lost all hope, the opposite of hopeful.

qa.q: What is situational irony?
qa.a: When what happens is the opposite of what was expected
qa.e: Situational irony is a gap between the expected result and the actual result.

qa.q: Stuck in a 3-hour traffic jam in Bengaluru, Kabir says, 'What a speedy ride!' What is this?
qa.e: Kabir says the opposite of what he means, which is verbal irony.

qa.q: In a school play, the audience knows the 'ghost' is just the cook in a bedsheet, but the hero shivers with fear. What is this?
qa.e: The audience knows something the character does not.

qa.q: A swimming coach slips into the pool and has to be rescued by his students. Which kind of irony is this?
qa.e: We expect a coach to rescue others, but the opposite happens.

qa.q: In 'A Letter to God', why is it ironic that the farmer calls the post office employees 'a bunch of crooks'?
qa.a: They were the ones who collected money to help him.
qa.e: The employees gave their own money; calling them crooks is the opposite of the truth.

qa.q: Which line shows verbal irony?
qa.a: 'Oh great, my phone died just when I needed the map.'
qa.e: 'Oh great' is said about a bad event, so the speaker means the opposite.

qa.q: Sarcasm is a sharp, mocking form of which kind of irony?
qa.e: Sarcasm is spoken, saying the opposite to mock, so it is verbal irony.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a type of irony?
qa.e: Alliteration is the repetition of the same starting sound; it is a sound device, not irony.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Dust of Snow' and 'Fire and Ice'?
qa.e: Both poems in the chapter are by Robert Frost.

qa.q: In 'Fire and Ice', what do fire and ice stand for?
qa.e: Fire symbolises desire and ice symbolises hatred.

qa.q: What is the central idea of 'Dust of Snow'?
qa.a: A small moment in nature can change a bad mood
qa.e: A crow shaking snow onto the poet lifts his mood and saves his day.

qa.q: Poem: A koel called from the neem tree, / Just when my sums went wrong; / My frown slipped off, I don't know how— / The day was saved by song. What is the rhyme scheme?
qa.e: Only lines 2 and 4 rhyme (wrong/song), so the scheme is abcb.

qa.q: Poem: A koel called from the neem tree, / Just when my sums went wrong; / My frown slipped off, I don't know how— / The day was saved by song. What changed the speaker's mood?
qa.e: The koel called and the frown slipped off; the day was 'saved by song'.

qa.q: What is a symbol in poetry?
qa.a: An object that stands for an idea beyond itself
qa.e: A symbol carries a deeper meaning, such as a dove for peace.

qa.q: In 'Dust of Snow', the crow and the hemlock tree are usually linked with what?
qa.e: Both are commonly seen as signs of gloom, yet here they bring a happy change.

qa.q: What does 'rue' mean?
qa.e: To rue something is to regret it.

qa.q: What was apartheid?
qa.a: A system of racial separation and discrimination in South Africa
qa.e: Apartheid kept people apart and treated them unequally by race.

qa.q: On which date was Nelson Mandela sworn in as President of South Africa?
qa.e: The inauguration took place on 10 May 1994; 1990 is the year he was released from prison.

qa.q: Passage: 'Freedom,' said Dadaji, 'is not only breaking your own chains. It is also making sure nobody else stays chained.' He spent his life teaching village children to read. According to Dadaji, what else does freedom mean?
qa.a: Making sure nobody else stays chained
qa.e: He says freedom is also making sure nobody else stays chained.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'Mandela ___ President in 1994.'
qa.e: 'In 1994' is a finished past time, so simple past is used.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'South Africa ___ a lot since apartheid ended.'
qa.e: 'Since' links the past to now, so present perfect is used.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'By the time he was freed, Mandela ___ 27 years in prison.'
qa.e: The prison years came before he was freed, so the earlier past action takes the past perfect.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'oppress'?
qa.e: -ion makes the noun; -ive makes an adjective; -ly makes an adverb; 'oppressful' is not a word.

qa.q: Which word is the opposite of 'freedom'?
qa.e: Bondage means being bound or enslaved; the others mean freedom.

qa.q: Who wrote 'A Tiger in the Zoo'?
qa.e: Leslie Norris wrote the poem.

qa.q: What is the main contrast in 'A Tiger in the Zoo'?
qa.a: The tiger's life in a cage and its life in the wild
qa.e: The poem sets the cage against the free forest life the tiger should have.

qa.q: Poem: The parakeet in the iron cage / Repeats the words we say; / But in his dreams the guava groves / Of Nashik call him away. Which device is used in 'guava groves'?
qa.e: The 'g' sound repeats at the start of both words.

qa.q: Poem: The parakeet in the iron cage / Repeats the words we say; / But in his dreams the guava groves / Of Nashik call him away. What does the parakeet dream of?
qa.e: Lines 3-4 say the guava groves of Nashik call him in his dreams.

qa.q: What is imagery?
qa.a: Language that creates pictures or feelings in the reader's mind
qa.e: Imagery appeals to the senses so we can picture a scene.

qa.q: What is enjambment?
qa.a: A sentence running on into the next line without a pause
qa.e: In enjambment the thought continues past the end of the line.

qa.q: What does 'captive' mean?
qa.a: Kept locked up and not free
qa.e: A captive animal is confined and not free.

qa.q: Which line best shows a contrast between captivity and freedom?
qa.a: 'Behind bars he paces; in the jungle he would roam.'
qa.e: It sets 'behind bars' against 'roam in the jungle', two opposite states.

qa.q: In 'His First Flight', what finally makes the young seagull fly?
qa.e: He is starving, dives at the food his mother holds out, and finds himself flying.

qa.q: Passage: Tara stood at the edge of the diving board in Pune. 'I can't do it,' she whispered. Her coach, Mr Rao, said, 'You can. I will be right here.' She shut her eyes, jumped, and came up laughing. How did Tara feel before the jump?
qa.e: She whispered 'I can't do it', which shows fear.

qa.q: Change to reported speech: She said, 'I can't do it.'
qa.a: She said that she couldn't do it.
qa.e: 'Can't' moves back to 'couldn't' and 'I' becomes 'she'.

qa.q: Change to reported speech: Mr Rao said, 'I will be right here.'
qa.a: Mr Rao said that he would be right there.
qa.e: 'Will' becomes 'would', 'I' becomes 'he', and 'here' becomes 'there'.

qa.q: In reported speech after 'said', 'today' usually becomes...
qa.e: 'Today' becomes 'that day' because the report is made at a later time.

qa.q: Change to reported speech: Ravi said, 'I am learning to swim.'
qa.a: Ravi said that he was learning to swim.
qa.e: Present continuous 'am learning' becomes past continuous 'was learning'.

qa.q: Which word means the same as 'timid'?
qa.e: Timid means shy and easily frightened.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'courage'?
qa.e: Cowardice is lack of courage.

qa.q: In 'The Black Aeroplane', what was strange about the plane that guided the pilot?
qa.a: The control tower said no other plane was flying
qa.e: The woman in the control tower said his was the only plane she could see on the radar, so the guide plane remains a mystery.

qa.q: Who tells the story in 'The Black Aeroplane'?
qa.e: It is a first-person story told by the pilot.

qa.q: Passage: At midnight, a soft tune drifted from the locked music room of the old Shimla guest house. In the morning, the caretaker, who kept the only key, found fresh rose petals on the piano keys. Choose the modal: 'The petals were fresh, so someone ___ have been in the room at night.'
qa.e: Fresh petals are strong evidence, so 'must have' shows near certainty.

qa.q: Choose the modal: 'The door was locked and the window was sealed, so the visitor ___ have left through them.'
qa.e: Both exits were closed, so it is impossible: 'can't have'.

qa.q: Choose the modal: 'Take an umbrella. It ___ rain later; the sky is getting cloudy.'
qa.e: Clouds make rain possible but not certain, so 'might' fits.

qa.q: Which modal shows the strongest certainty?
qa.e: 'Must' in deduction means the speaker is almost sure.

qa.q: What does 'mysterious' mean?
qa.e: Something mysterious puzzles us because we cannot explain it.

qa.q: Which word means 'completely puzzled'?
qa.e: Baffled means totally puzzled.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Ball Poem'?
qa.e: John Berryman wrote 'The Ball Poem'.

qa.q: What does the boy in 'The Ball Poem' learn?
qa.a: That loss is part of life and he must learn to bear it
qa.e: Losing the ball teaches him, for the first time, what loss means.

qa.q: Why does the poet in 'The Ball Poem' not buy the boy another ball?
qa.a: He wants the boy to learn to accept loss himself
qa.e: Money can't replace what is lost; the boy must learn responsibility for his feelings.

qa.q: Poem: My kite snapped free above the Jaipur roofs / And drifted past the sun; / I cried, then learnt that some things go— / And growing up's begun. What has the speaker learnt?
qa.a: Some things are lost for good, and that is part of growing up
qa.e: The speaker says 'some things go' and 'growing up's begun'.

qa.q: Poem: My kite snapped free above the Jaipur roofs / And drifted past the sun; / I cried, then learnt that some things go— / And growing up's begun. What is the rhyme scheme?
qa.e: Only 'sun' and 'begun' (lines 2 and 4) rhyme.

qa.q: What is the tone of 'How to Tell Wild Animals' by Carolyn Wells?
qa.e: It gives silly, exaggerated ways to identify animals, which makes it funny.

qa.q: What is 'tone' in a poem?
qa.a: The writer's attitude or feeling shown through the words
qa.e: Tone tells us how the writer feels about the subject.

qa.q: Which word means the same as 'grief'?
qa.e: Grief and sorrow both mean deep sadness.

qa.q: What name did Anne Frank give her diary?
qa.e: Anne addressed her diary as 'Kitty', like a friend.

qa.q: Why did Anne decide to keep a diary?
qa.a: She felt she had no true friend to confide in
qa.e: She had many acquaintances but no real friend to share her thoughts with.

qa.q: Why did Mr Keesing give Anne extra essays to write?
qa.a: She talked too much in class
qa.e: He kept punishing her chattering with extra essays.

qa.q: What goes at the very top of a diary entry?
qa.e: A diary begins with the date, day and time.

qa.q: A diary entry is usually written in which person?
qa.e: The writer speaks about herself or himself: I, me, my.

qa.q: What is the tone of a diary entry?
qa.e: A diary is a private conversation with oneself.

qa.q: Diary: Monday, 3 March, 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today Miss Iyer made me read my poem aloud. My voice shook at first, but the whole class clapped! I might write another one tonight. — Pihu What made Pihu happy?
qa.a: The whole class clapped for her poem
qa.e: She writes that the whole class clapped, followed by an exclamation mark.

qa.q: Diary: Monday, 3 March, 9 p.m. Dear Diary, Today Miss Iyer made me read my poem aloud. My voice shook at first, but the whole class clapped! I might write another one tonight. — Pihu Which detail of diary format is missing in Pihu's entry?
qa.e: The entry has the day, date, time, 'Dear Diary', the body and her name.

qa.q: In which years was the Second World War fought?
qa.e: WWII began in 1939 and ended in 1945; 1914-1918 was the First World War.

qa.q: In which city did Anne Frank's family go into hiding?
qa.e: The family lived and hid in Amsterdam in the Netherlands.

qa.q: Who published Anne Frank's diary after the war?
qa.e: Her father survived and published her diary.

qa.q: Report: Mr Keesing asked Anne, 'Are you talking again?'
qa.a: Mr Keesing asked Anne whether she was talking again.
qa.e: A yes/no question is reported with 'whether', statement order and no question mark.

qa.q: Report: She asked me, 'Where do you live?'
qa.a: She asked me where I lived.
qa.e: Keep 'where', put subject before verb, and shift live → lived.

qa.q: Which word introduces a reported yes/no question?
qa.e: Yes/no questions are reported with 'if' or 'whether'.

qa.q: Report: The principal said to Rohan, 'Why are you late?'
qa.a: The principal asked Rohan why he was late.
qa.e: 'Said to' becomes 'asked' for a question; then wh-word + statement order.

qa.q: Which sentence is correct?
qa.a: He asked me where the station was.
qa.e: In reported questions the subject comes before the verb: 'the station was'.

qa.q: Who wrote the poem 'Amanda!'?
qa.e: 'Amanda!' is by Robin Klein.

qa.q: Why does Amanda daydream of being a mermaid or Rapunzel?
qa.a: To escape the constant instructions and feel free
qa.e: Her daydreams are an escape from nagging into a world of freedom.

qa.q: In 'Amanda!', who is most likely giving Amanda all the instructions?
qa.e: The commands about manners and chores come from an adult at home, usually taken to be her mother.

qa.q: Poem: Sit straight, Ishaan! Don't swing your feet! / (I'm a falcon over Ladakh's peaks.) / Finish your milk and comb your hair! / (Up here there's only sky and air.) What do the lines in brackets show?
qa.e: They describe flying over Ladakh, which happens only in his imagination.

qa.q: What type of sentence is 'Don't swing your feet!'?
qa.e: It gives a command; the exclamation mark adds force but it is still an imperative.

qa.q: Which is an exclamatory sentence?
qa.e: It expresses a strong feeling and begins with 'What a ...'.

qa.q: What does 'nag' mean?
qa.e: To nag is to keep finding fault or telling someone what to do.

qa.q: Poem: Sit straight, Ishaan! Don't swing your feet! / (I'm a falcon over Ladakh's peaks.) / Finish your milk and comb your hair! / (Up here there's only sky and air.) What is the tone of the lines that are not in brackets?
qa.e: They are a stream of commands, which sounds bossy.

qa.q: What are traditional bakers called in Goa, as described in 'Glimpses of India'?
qa.e: Goan bakers are known as paders.

qa.q: Goa's tradition of baking bread is linked to the rule of which European power?
qa.e: Goa was a Portuguese colony, and baking bread came with that period.

qa.q: Passage: When Nani was a girl in Margao, the baker used to come every morning with a basket of warm bread on his head. The children would rush to the gate the moment they heard his horn, hoping for a sweet bun. What did the children hope for?
qa.e: The last words say they hoped for a sweet bun.

qa.q: What does 'used to' show in 'He used to come every morning'?
qa.a: A past habit that no longer happens
qa.e: 'Used to' describes a regular action in the past.

qa.q: Choose the correct sentence.
qa.a: Did you use to play cricket in school?
qa.e: After 'did', the base form 'use to' is used.

qa.q: Choose the correct word: 'Long ago, on festival days, Nani ___ bake cakes for the whole street.'
qa.e: 'Would' shows a repeated action in the past.

qa.q: Which sentence uses 'would' wrongly?
qa.a: I would have a dog called Tommy when I was young.
qa.e: 'Having a dog' is a past state, so 'used to have' is needed; 'would' is only for repeated actions.

qa.q: What does 'nostalgia' mean?
qa.a: A warm, longing feeling for the past
qa.e: Nostalgia is a fond, slightly sad longing for the past.

qa.q: In which state is Coorg (Kodagu)?
qa.e: Coorg is a district of Karnataka.

qa.q: Which river rises in the hills of Coorg?
qa.e: The Kaveri begins in the Coorg hills.

qa.q: Which pairing is correct?
qa.e: Coorg is known for coffee and Assam for tea.

qa.q: Who are the two friends in 'Tea from Assam'?
qa.e: Pranjol and Rajvir travel to Assam together.

qa.q: According to one legend in 'Tea from Assam', how was tea discovered?
qa.a: Leaves fell into a Chinese emperor's pot of boiling water
qa.e: The legend says a few leaves dropped into the emperor's boiling water and gave it a pleasant flavour.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'Assam is ___ than Goa.'
qa.e: Two places are compared, so the comparative 'bigger' is used.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'Of all the hill stations we visited, Madikeri was the ___.'
qa.e: 'Of all' compares more than two, so the superlative is needed.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'This tea is good, but the tea at the estate was even ___.'
qa.e: 'Good' is irregular: good-better-best; comparing two teas needs 'better'.

qa.q: Passage: We reached Munnar by noon. Mist curled over the rolling green tea hills, and the air smelled of cardamom. A tiny old wooden stall sold hot banana fritters that crackled in the pan. Which detail appeals to the sense of smell?
qa.e: 'Smelled of cardamom' is about smell.

qa.q: Passage: We reached Munnar by noon. Mist curled over the rolling green tea hills, and the air smelled of cardamom. A tiny old wooden stall sold hot banana fritters that crackled in the pan. Which detail appeals to hearing?
qa.a: Fritters that crackled in the pan
qa.e: 'Crackled' is a sound.

qa.q: Which phrase has the adjectives in the correct order?
qa.e: Size (tiny) comes before age (old), which comes before material (wooden).

qa.q: Which phrase is in the correct order?
qa.a: a lovely little red Kashmiri shawl
qa.e: Opinion, size, colour, origin: lovely, little, red, Kashmiri.

qa.q: What makes a travel description lively?
qa.a: Sensory details and the writer's impressions
qa.e: Details and feelings help readers picture and feel the place.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Trees'?
qa.e: 'The Trees' is by Adrienne Rich.

qa.q: What does 'The Trees' suggest when the trees move out into the forest?
qa.a: Living things long to be free
qa.e: The trees leave the house to return to the forest, showing a desire for freedom.

qa.q: Which line uses personification?
qa.a: The wind whispered through the pines.
qa.e: Whispering is a human action given to the wind.

qa.q: From which country did Gavin Maxwell bring Mijbil the otter?
qa.e: Maxwell got Mij in southern Iraq and later took him to London.

qa.q: Why was Mij's kind of otter named after Gavin Maxwell?
qa.a: It had not been known to science before
qa.e: It was a new race of otter, so it was named Maxwell's otter.

qa.q: Passage: Our puppy, Laddoo, and our old cat, Mishri, share the sunny corner of the verandah. Neither of them likes the noisy mixer. Every morning, the pair races to the kitchen when the milk boils. Choose the correct verb: 'Neither of them ___ the noisy mixer.'
qa.e: 'Neither of' takes a singular verb.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Laddoo and Mishri ___ the corner of the verandah.'
qa.e: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'One of my pets ___ a parrot.'
qa.e: The subject is 'one', so the verb is singular.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'The teacher, along with her students, ___ visiting the zoo.'
qa.e: With 'along with', the verb agrees with the first subject, 'the teacher'.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Either the cats or the dog ___ broken the vase.'
qa.e: With 'either...or', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the dog'.

qa.q: Passage: Our puppy, Laddoo, and our old cat, Mishri, share the sunny corner of the verandah. Neither of them likes the noisy mixer. Every morning, the pair races to the kitchen when the milk boils. What do the pets do when the milk boils?
qa.e: The last line says the pair races to the kitchen.

qa.q: In 'Mijbil the Otter', what did Mij love most?
qa.e: Mij spent hours splashing and playing in water.

qa.q: How did Mij travel to London?
qa.a: By plane, packed in a box
qa.e: Mij was packed in a box and flown to London.

qa.q: Passage: The otter on the Chambal bank slid down the mud, splashed into the river, and bobbed up with a fish, chirping happily. Then it rolled over and over on the warm sand. What sound did the otter make?
qa.e: The passage says it was 'chirping happily'.

qa.q: Which verb best describes how a snake moves?
qa.e: Snakes slide along the ground: they slither.

qa.q: Which verb best describes how a duck walks?
qa.e: Ducks walk with a side-to-side sway: they waddle.

qa.q: Which verb best describes a tiger moving quietly while hunting?
qa.e: To prowl is to move quietly and secretly, looking for prey.

qa.q: Choose the adverb: 'The otter swam ___ through the water.'
qa.e: An adverb describes the verb 'swam'; graceful + -ly = gracefully.

qa.q: Which word means 'playful and full of fun'?
qa.e: Frolicsome means lively and playful.

qa.q: Who wrote the poem 'Fog'?
qa.e: 'Fog' is by Carl Sandburg.

qa.q: In 'Fog', what is the fog compared to?
qa.e: The fog moves silently, sits and moves on like a cat.

qa.q: What is a metaphor?
qa.a: A direct comparison that says one thing is another
qa.e: A metaphor compares without 'like' or 'as'.

qa.q: 'Her smile is sunshine.' What figure of speech is this?
qa.e: It says the smile IS sunshine, with no 'like' or 'as'.

qa.q: 'He runs like a cheetah.' What figure of speech is this?
qa.e: It compares using 'like', so it is a simile.

qa.q: Poem: Evening is a grey heron / Standing still on one leg; / It folds the river in its wings / And flies off into the night. What is evening compared to?
qa.e: Line 1 says 'Evening is a grey heron'.

qa.q: Why is the comparison in 'Fog' a metaphor rather than a simile?
qa.e: Similes need 'like' or 'as'; the fog is described as a cat directly.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT a metaphor?
qa.a: The baby slept like a log.
qa.e: 'Like a log' uses 'like', so it is a simile.

qa.q: In 'Madam Rides the Bus', what is Valli's greatest wish?
qa.a: To ride the bus to the town
qa.e: Valli longs to travel on the bus she watches every day.

qa.q: How does Valli get the money for her bus ride?
qa.a: She saves her coins carefully over a long time
qa.e: She saves every coin and resists spending on treats.

qa.q: Passage: Chintu pressed his nose to the bus window in Chennai. 'Uncle, please open the window wider,' he said to the conductor. 'Don't lean out,' the conductor warned, smiling. Report what the conductor said.
qa.a: The conductor warned Chintu not to lean out.
qa.e: Negative command: warned + person + not to + verb.

qa.q: Passage: Chintu pressed his nose to the bus window in Chennai. 'Uncle, please open the window wider,' he said to the conductor. 'Don't lean out,' the conductor warned, smiling. Report what Chintu said.
qa.a: Chintu requested the conductor to open the window wider.
qa.e: 'Please' signals a request; the reporting verb 'requested' replaces it.

qa.q: Report: Mother said to me, 'You should carry water.'
qa.a: Mother advised me to carry water.
qa.e: 'Should' gives advice, so 'advised + to + verb' is used.

qa.q: Which reporting verb best suits a polite request?
qa.e: A request is reported with 'requested'.

qa.q: What does 'curious' mean?
qa.e: A curious person wants to find out about things.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'curious'?
qa.e: The noun is 'curiosity' (note the spelling: no 'u' after 's').

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon'?
qa.e: Ogden Nash wrote this funny ballad.

qa.q: What is a ballad?
qa.a: A poem that tells a story, usually in rhyming stanzas
qa.e: Ballads are story poems with regular rhyme and rhythm.

qa.q: How do the others describe Custard at the start?
qa.e: Custard is mocked for being a coward who cries for a safe cage.

qa.q: What is the name of Belinda's dog?
qa.e: Mustard is the dog; Ink is the kitten, Blink the mouse, Custard the dragon.

qa.q: What is the rhyme scheme of 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon'?
qa.e: Each pair of lines rhymes: aabb.

qa.q: Ballad: In Madurai lived a girl named Meera, / With a parrot called Pista and a goat called Heera, / And a timid old buffalo, slow as a snail, / Who once chased a thief all the way to the jail! What makes this ballad funny?
qa.a: A timid, slow buffalo chases a thief to jail
qa.e: The surprise that the 'timid', slow buffalo becomes a hero is the joke.
