qa.q: Ballad: In Madurai lived a girl named Meera, / With a parrot called Pista and a goat called Heera, / And a timid old buffalo, slow as a snail, / Who once chased a thief all the way to the jail! Which phrase is a simile?
qa.e: It compares using 'as'.

qa.q: What is the funny twist in 'The Tale of Custard the Dragon'?
qa.a: The 'cowardly' dragon is the only one who fights the pirate
qa.e: Those who boasted of courage hide, and Custard fights.

qa.q: Whose teaching is described in 'The Sermon at Benares'?
qa.e: The lesson is about the Buddha and Kisa Gotami.

qa.q: What did the Buddha ask Kisa Gotami to bring?
qa.a: Mustard seed from a house where no one had died
qa.e: He asked for mustard seed from a house that had never known death.

qa.q: What did Kisa Gotami finally understand?
qa.e: No house was free of death, so she saw that loss is common to all.

qa.q: Passage: When Arjun's grandfather passed away, Arjun shut himself in his room. His aunt sat beside him and said gently, 'Every family we know has lost someone. Grief shared is grief halved.' Slowly, Arjun opened the window. What did the aunt's words mean?
qa.a: Sharing sorrow makes it easier to bear
qa.e: 'Grief shared is grief halved' means sorrow feels lighter when shared.

qa.q: Choose the connector: 'Arjun was sad. ___, he went to school.'
qa.e: Going to school despite being sad shows contrast: 'However'.

qa.q: Choose the connector: 'She could not find the seed ___ every house had lost someone.'
qa.e: The second part gives the reason, so 'because' fits.

qa.q: Choose the connector: '___ it was raining, they went to the fair.'
qa.e: Going despite rain is a contrast: 'Although'.

qa.q: What does 'console' mean?
qa.e: To console is to comfort in grief or disappointment.

qa.q: Who wrote 'For Anne Gregory'?
qa.e: The poem is by the Irish poet W.B. Yeats.

qa.q: What does the young woman in 'For Anne Gregory' want?
qa.a: To be loved for herself, not for her yellow hair
qa.e: She wants to be valued for who she is inside.

qa.q: What is the main theme of 'For Anne Gregory'?
qa.e: The poem contrasts being loved for looks with being loved for oneself.

qa.q: Poem: 'Don't praise my curls,' my sister said, / 'Praise the kindness that I do.' / Dadi laughed, 'Child, most eyes will see / Your curls before they look at you.' What does the sister want praised?
qa.e: She says, 'Praise the kindness that I do.'

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'visible'?
qa.e: 'Visible' takes the prefix in-: invisible.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'honest'?
qa.e: 'Honest' takes the prefix dis-.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'responsible'?
qa.e: Words starting with r often take ir-: irresponsible.

qa.q: What does 'superficial' mean?
qa.a: Only on the surface; not deep
qa.e: Superficial means concerned only with what is on the outside.

qa.q: What is a one-act play?
qa.a: A short play with one act, few characters and usually one setting
qa.e: A one-act play is complete in a single act.

qa.q: What are stage directions?
qa.a: Instructions about how characters act or speak
qa.e: They guide actors' movements and tone, often in brackets.

qa.q: What is a farce?
qa.a: A comedy with exaggerated characters and silly situations
qa.e: Farce uses exaggeration and absurd situations to make people laugh.

qa.q: Scene: RAHUL (nervously): Uncle, I have come to ask... to ask... / MR VERMA (smiling): Speak up, beta! / RAHUL (clutching his chest): My heart is pounding! What do the words in brackets tell us?
qa.a: How the characters speak and act
qa.e: '(nervously)', '(smiling)' are stage directions.

qa.q: In 'The Proposal', why does Lomov visit Chubukov's house?
qa.e: He arrives in formal dress to propose to Natalya.

qa.q: What do Lomov and Natalya quarrel about first?
qa.e: The first quarrel is over who owns the Oxen Meadows; the dog quarrel comes later.

qa.q: What is the second big quarrel in 'The Proposal' about?
qa.e: Lomov's dog Guess and the Chubukovs' dog Squeezer are compared.

qa.q: Scene: RAHUL (nervously): Uncle, I have come to ask... to ask... / MR VERMA (smiling): Speak up, beta! / RAHUL (clutching his chest): My heart is pounding! Report: Mr Verma said to Rahul, 'Speak up, beta!'
qa.a: Mr Verma affectionately told Rahul to speak up.
qa.e: A command is reported with told + person + to + verb; 'beta' is replaced by 'affectionately'.

qa.q: What was Anton Chekhov's nationality?
qa.e: Chekhov was a Russian playwright and short-story writer.

qa.q: Besides writing, what was Chekhov's profession?
qa.e: Chekhov trained and worked as a doctor.

qa.q: Chekhov is best known for which kinds of writing?
qa.e: He is famous for his plays and short stories.

qa.q: What does Lomov keep complaining about in 'The Proposal'?
qa.a: His health, such as palpitations and a numb leg
qa.e: He keeps mentioning palpitations and other aches.

qa.q: What is a hypochondriac?
qa.a: Someone who worries too much about their health
qa.e: A hypochondriac fears being ill even without real cause.

qa.q: What does 'quarrelsome' mean?
qa.e: -some here means 'tending to': quarrelsome = tending to quarrel.

qa.q: What mainly makes 'The Proposal' comic?
qa.a: The characters quarrel over trifles instead of getting on with the proposal
qa.e: Exaggerated quarrels over small matters keep delaying the proposal.

qa.q: Which is the adjective form of 'humour'?
qa.e: Humour + -ous gives 'humorous' (note the spelling drops the 'u').

qa.q: Who is Tricki Woo in 'A Triumph of Surgery'?
qa.e: Tricki Woo is Mrs Pumphrey's pampered little dog.

qa.q: Why does Tricki fall ill?
qa.a: He is over-fed and gets too little exercise
qa.e: Too many rich treats and no exercise make him fat and sick.

qa.q: How does the vet cure Tricki?
qa.a: With a strict diet and plenty of play with other dogs
qa.e: No food for two days, then simple food and exercise with other dogs, cure him.

qa.q: Change to passive: 'Mrs Pumphrey fed Tricki cream cakes.'
qa.a: Tricki was fed cream cakes by Mrs Pumphrey.
qa.e: Past active 'fed' becomes past passive 'was fed'.

qa.q: Change to passive: 'The vet examines the dog.'
qa.a: The dog is examined by the vet.
qa.e: Simple present: is + past participle.

qa.q: Change to passive: 'They have taken Bruno to the vet.'
qa.a: Bruno has been taken to the vet.
qa.e: Present perfect passive: has been + past participle; 'they' can be left out.

qa.q: Passage: Bruno, a spoilt beagle in Bandra, was given jalebis and ice cream every day. Soon he was too fat to climb the stairs. He was taken to the vet, was put on a strict diet, and was made to run in the park. What happened to Bruno at the vet?
qa.a: He was put on a strict diet and made to run
qa.e: The last line says he was put on a strict diet and made to run in the park.

qa.q: What does 'pampered' mean?
qa.a: Given too much care and comfort; spoiled
qa.e: A pampered pet is spoiled with too much attention and treats.

qa.q: Why is the title 'A Triumph of Surgery' humorous?
qa.a: No surgery was done; diet and exercise cured the dog
qa.e: The 'triumph' came from simple care, not an operation, which is ironic.

qa.q: Who narrates 'A Triumph of Surgery'?
qa.e: The story is told in the first person by the vet.

qa.q: What was James Herriot's profession?
qa.e: Herriot was a vet who wrote stories about his animal patients.

qa.q: What does 'in the pink of health' mean?
qa.e: It is an idiom meaning very healthy.

qa.q: What does 'let the cat out of the bag' mean?
qa.e: It means to reveal a secret, often accidentally.

qa.q: 'Mrs Kapoor feeds her pug enough laddoos to feed a whole wedding!' Which device is this?
qa.e: It is deliberate exaggeration for effect.

qa.q: What does 'over the moon' mean?
qa.e: Being over the moon means being delighted.

qa.q: Which sentence uses an idiom correctly?
qa.a: The maths test was a piece of cake, so I finished early.
qa.e: 'A piece of cake' means very easy, which fits finishing early.

qa.q: Who narrates 'The Thief's Story'?
qa.e: The thief, Hari Singh, tells the story in the first person.

qa.q: Who wrote 'The Thief's Story'?
qa.e: Ruskin Bond wrote this story.

qa.q: What does Anil teach Hari?
qa.e: Anil teaches Hari to read and write, which changes Hari's life.

qa.q: Why does Hari return the money?
qa.a: He realises that learning and Anil's trust are worth more than money
qa.e: He sees that education could make him a respected man, and he values Anil's trust.

qa.q: Passage: While Anil was sleeping, Hari crept to the mattress. He had already decided to run away. But at the station, as the train was leaving, he remembered Anil's kindness and turned back. Choose the tense of 'was sleeping'.
qa.e: was/were + -ing = past continuous, for background action.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'By the time Hari reached the station, the train ___.'
qa.e: The train left before he reached, so past perfect is used for the earlier action.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'We ___ cricket when it started to rain.'
qa.e: The longer background action takes past continuous; the interruption takes simple past.

qa.q: Passage: While Anil was sleeping, Hari crept to the mattress. He had already decided to run away. But at the station, as the train was leaving, he remembered Anil's kindness and turned back. What made Hari turn back?
qa.e: The last line says he remembered Anil's kindness and turned back.

qa.q: Which trait best describes Anil in 'The Thief's Story'?
qa.e: He gives a stranger work and keeps trusting him.

qa.q: How does Hari change in 'The Thief's Story'?
qa.a: From a thief to someone who values education and trust
qa.e: He returns the money, choosing learning and trust over theft.

qa.q: What does 'remorse' mean?
qa.e: Remorse is the guilty sorrow felt after doing something wrong.

qa.q: What does 'reform' mean?
qa.e: To reform is to improve one's behaviour.

qa.q: What does 'conscience' mean?
qa.a: An inner sense of right and wrong
qa.e: Conscience is the inner voice that tells right from wrong.

qa.q: What should a character sketch include?
qa.a: Traits supported by evidence from the story
qa.e: Each trait needs an example from the story to support it.

qa.q: Which sentence gives a trait WITH evidence?
qa.a: Meera is generous: she shared her lunch with a new classmate on her first day.
qa.e: It names a trait and backs it with an action.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'trust'?
qa.e: 'Distrust' means lack of trust; 'entrust' means to hand over responsibility.

qa.q: Who is Ausable in 'The Midnight Visitor'?
qa.a: A secret agent who does not look like a typical spy
qa.e: Ausable is a fat, plain-looking secret agent.

qa.q: Who is Fowler in 'The Midnight Visitor'?
qa.a: A young writer who expected spies to be glamorous
qa.e: Fowler is a writer disappointed by Ausable's ordinary looks.

qa.q: Who is waiting in Ausable's room with a pistol?
qa.e: Max, a rival agent, has come for a secret paper.

qa.q: What story does Ausable invent to trick Max?
qa.a: That there is a balcony below the window
qa.e: He says there is a balcony and that police are coming, so Max will try to hide there.

qa.q: Which is a typical feature of a spy story?
qa.e: Spy stories build suspense around secret missions.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'If the police ___, they will search the room.'
qa.e: First conditional: If + present, will + verb.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'If I ___ a spy, I would carry a secret camera.'
qa.e: Second conditional for imaginary situations: If + past ('were').

qa.q: Passage: Agent Kavya noticed that the 'courier' wore shiny, spotless shoes on a muddy Cherrapunji morning. She smiled, handed him an empty envelope, and quietly alerted her team. What clue made Kavya suspicious?
qa.a: His spotless shoes on a muddy morning
qa.e: Spotless shoes did not fit a muddy morning; she was the one who handed over the empty envelope.

qa.q: How does Ausable get rid of Max?
qa.a: He invents a balcony and says the police are coming
qa.e: His made-up story makes Max climb out of the window.

qa.q: Who was knocking at the door in 'The Midnight Visitor'?
qa.e: The knock was a waiter with the drinks Ausable had ordered.

qa.q: What does 'presence of mind' mean?
qa.a: Thinking calmly and quickly in an emergency
qa.e: It is the ability to stay calm and act wisely in a crisis.

qa.q: What does 'think on your feet' mean?
qa.e: It is an idiom for quick thinking in a situation.

qa.q: What does 'bluff' mean?
qa.e: Ausable bluffs about the balcony and the police.

qa.q: Which word best signals a surprise in a story?
qa.e: 'Suddenly' introduces something unexpected.

qa.q: What does 'composed' mean when describing a person?
qa.e: A composed person stays calm, like Ausable.

qa.q: Which action best shows quick thinking?
qa.a: When the lift stopped, Neha pressed the alarm and calmly asked everyone to stay still.
qa.e: She stayed calm and did the safe, sensible thing.

qa.q: Why does Horace Danby steal in 'A Question of Trust'?
qa.a: To buy rare and expensive books
qa.e: He robs one safe a year and spends the money on rare books.

qa.q: What is Horace Danby's regular job?
qa.e: He is a respected locksmith, which helps him open safes.

qa.q: Who tricks Horace into opening the safe?
qa.a: A young woman pretending to be the lady of the house
qa.e: She pretends the house is hers and asks him to open the safe.

qa.q: Why is Horace caught?
qa.a: His fingerprints are found on the safe
qa.e: He had taken off his gloves, so his fingerprints were on the safe.

qa.q: What is the main irony in 'A Question of Trust'?
qa.a: A clever thief is himself cheated by another thief
qa.e: Horace, who fooled everyone, is fooled by the woman.

qa.q: Passage: Mr Bose, who sells 'unbreakable' anti-theft locks in Kolkata, returned from his shop one evening to find that his own scooter had been stolen from outside his house. What type of irony is this?
qa.e: A lock seller being robbed is the opposite of what we expect.

qa.q: What does 'As you sow, so shall you reap' mean?
qa.a: You face the results of your own actions
qa.e: The proverb uses farming to say actions bring matching results.

qa.q: Which proverb best fits Horace's fate?
qa.a: As you sow, so shall you reap.
qa.e: Horace's dishonest actions bring him punishment.

qa.q: What is a 'burglary'?
qa.a: Breaking into a building to steal
qa.e: Burglary is entering a building illegally to steal.

qa.q: What is an 'accomplice'?
qa.a: A person who helps someone commit a crime
qa.e: An accomplice is a partner in a crime.

qa.q: What is an 'alibi'?
qa.a: Proof that someone was elsewhere when a crime happened
qa.e: An alibi shows a suspect could not have done it.

qa.q: Who is a 'suspect'?
qa.a: A person thought to have committed a crime
qa.e: A suspect is believed, but not yet proven, to be guilty.

qa.q: What should the first paragraph of a news report answer?
qa.a: Who, what, when, where, why and how
qa.e: The lead gives the key facts (5Ws and 1H).

qa.q: News: Pune, 12 March: A locksmith was arrested on Tuesday after police found his fingerprints on a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow. Jewellery worth lakhs is missing. Where was the safe?
qa.a: In a bungalow in Koregaon Park
qa.e: The report says 'a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow'.

qa.q: News: Pune, 12 March: A locksmith was arrested on Tuesday after police found his fingerprints on a safe in a Koregaon Park bungalow. Jewellery worth lakhs is missing. Why does the report say 'was arrested' instead of naming who arrested him?
qa.a: The passive voice keeps the focus on the person arrested
qa.e: News reports often use the passive to focus on what happened to someone.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'guilty'?
qa.e: Innocent means not guilty.

qa.q: Who wrote 'Footprints without Feet'?
qa.e: It is adapted from H.G. Wells's 'The Invisible Man'.

qa.q: Who is Griffin?
qa.a: A scientist who made himself invisible
qa.e: Griffin is the scientist whose experiment made him invisible.

qa.q: How did Griffin become invisible?
qa.e: He swallowed rare drugs that made his body transparent.

qa.q: What did the two boys in London see?
qa.a: Fresh muddy footprints with no one there
qa.e: They saw footprints appearing on the steps without anyone visible.

qa.q: What does 'transparent' mean?
qa.e: Transparent things, like clear glass, let us see through them.

qa.q: What does 'opaque' mean?
qa.e: Opaque objects, like wood, block light completely.

qa.q: What does the prefix 'in-' mean in 'invisible'?
qa.e: Invisible = not visible.

qa.q: Passage: The new glass door at the mall was so clean and transparent that Bunty walked straight into it. He rubbed his nose while his sister giggled behind him. Why did Bunty walk into the door?
qa.a: It was so transparent that he did not see it
qa.e: The passage links the clean, transparent glass with his bump.

qa.q: What is the central message of 'Footprints without Feet'?
qa.a: A great scientific discovery can be harmful if used without ethics
qa.e: Griffin's misuse of his discovery shows the need for responsibility.

qa.q: How does Griffin misuse his invisibility?
qa.a: He uses it to steal and frighten people
qa.e: He becomes a lawless man who robs and scares people.

qa.q: What does 'ethics' mean?
qa.a: Moral principles of right and wrong
qa.e: Ethics deals with what is morally right or wrong.

qa.q: Which complimentary close suits a letter to the editor?
qa.e: Formal letters to editors end with 'Yours faithfully' (or 'Yours truly').

qa.q: In a formal letter, what comes immediately before the salutation?
qa.e: The order is: receiver's address, subject, salutation.

qa.q: Which salutation is right for a letter to the editor?
qa.e: Formal letters use 'Sir/Madam'.

qa.q: Which is the best subject line for a letter to the editor?
qa.a: Subject: Loudspeakers played late at night in residential areas
qa.e: It is short, clear and names the issue.

qa.q: What tone should a letter to the editor have?
qa.e: Even when complaining, the tone stays formal and respectful.

qa.q: Which insects fascinated Richard Ebright as a child?
qa.e: He collected butterflies, especially monarchs.

qa.q: Which book did his mother give Ebright?
qa.e: This book about monarch migration started his tagging work.

qa.q: Who encouraged Ebright the most as a child?
qa.e: His mother took him on trips and bought him science books and equipment.

qa.q: What did Ebright's viceroy butterfly project test?
qa.e: He tested the theory that viceroys copy (mimic) monarchs.

qa.q: Which is one quality the lesson says makes a scientist?
qa.e: The lesson lists a first-rate mind, curiosity, and the will to win for the right reasons.

qa.q: What is the adjective form of 'science'?
qa.e: 'Scientist' is a person (noun); 'scientific' is the adjective.

qa.q: What does 'mimic' mean?
qa.e: To mimic is to copy something's look or behaviour.

qa.q: What does 'fascinated' mean?
qa.e: Fascinated means deeply interested.

qa.q: Data: Science club members at Sunrise School: 2021: 20, 2022: 28, 2023: 35, 2024: 33, 2025: 50. In which year was membership the highest?
qa.e: 50 members in 2025 is the highest figure.

qa.q: Data: Science club members at Sunrise School: 2021: 20, 2022: 28, 2023: 35, 2024: 33, 2025: 50. By how many members did the club grow from 2021 to 2025?
Data: Science club members at Sunrise School: 2021: 20, 2022: 28, 2023: 35, 2024: 33, 2025: 50. In which year did membership fall?
qa.e: It went from 35 in 2023 down to 33 in 2024.

qa.q: What does 'membership doubled' mean?
qa.e: To double is to become two times as much.

qa.q: How should an analytical paragraph begin?
qa.a: With an introduction saying what the data is about
qa.e: The opening tells the reader what the chart shows and the period.

qa.q: Which sentence best suits an analytical paragraph?
qa.a: Membership rose steadily from 20 in 2021 to 35 in 2023.
qa.e: It describes a trend with exact figures, with no opinion.

qa.q: What does 'fluctuate' mean?
qa.e: Fluctuating figures go up and down.

qa.q: Which question shows scientific curiosity?
qa.a: Why do the leaves of the touch-me-not plant fold when touched?
qa.e: It asks 'why' about a natural event and can be investigated.

qa.q: What nationality was Guy de Maupassant?
qa.e: Maupassant was a French writer.

qa.q: Maupassant is famous for short stories with what kind of endings?
qa.e: His stories often end with an unexpected twist.

qa.q: What does Matilda borrow from Madame Forestier?
qa.e: She borrows what she believes is a diamond necklace.

qa.q: What is the twist at the end of 'The Necklace'?
qa.e: After years of hardship, Matilda learns it was worth very little.

qa.q: Passage: Rani, who loved to look rich, borrowed her cousin's silk sari for a wedding in Lucknow. The sari, which she wore proudly, tore on a nail. She worked for months to buy a new one, only to hear her cousin laugh, 'That was a cheap copy!' Choose the relative pronoun: 'Rani, ___ loved to look rich, borrowed a sari.'
qa.e: 'Who' is used for people; 'that' cannot begin a clause set off by commas.

qa.q: Choose the relative pronoun: 'The sari, ___ she wore proudly, tore on a nail.'
qa.e: 'Which' is used for things in a clause set off by commas.

qa.q: Join: 'The woman laughed. Rani had borrowed the woman's sari.'
qa.a: The woman whose sari Rani had borrowed laughed.
qa.e: 'Whose' shows possession: the woman's sari.

qa.q: Passage: Rani, who loved to look rich, borrowed her cousin's silk sari for a wedding in Lucknow. The sari, which she wore proudly, tore on a nail. She worked for months to buy a new one, only to hear her cousin laugh, 'That was a cheap copy!' What is the twist in Rani's story?
qa.a: The sari she replaced was only a cheap copy
qa.e: Her cousin's laugh reveals it was a cheap copy, so her months of work were needless.

qa.q: What is 'vanity'?
qa.a: Too much pride in one's looks or status
qa.e: Vanity is excessive pride in oneself or one's appearance.

qa.q: Why does Matilda borrow the necklace?
qa.a: To look rich and elegant at a party
qa.e: She wants to impress others at the party.

qa.q: How long do the Loisels work to repay their debt?
qa.e: They spend 10 years in hardship.

qa.q: What could have saved the Loisels from years of hardship?
qa.e: Honesty would have revealed the necklace was fake.

qa.q: What is the abstract noun of 'vain'?
qa.e: The noun is 'vanity'; 'vainly' is an adverb and 'vainity' is a misspelling.

qa.q: What is the abstract noun of 'humble'?
qa.e: 'Humility' is the abstract noun; 'humbly' is an adverb and 'humblity' is a misspelling.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'vanity'?
qa.e: Modesty means not boasting about oneself.

qa.q: What does 'contentment' mean?
qa.a: Being satisfied with what one has
qa.e: Contentment is a peaceful feeling of satisfaction.

qa.q: What is Bholi's real name?
qa.e: 'Bholi' is a nickname; her real name is Sulekha.

qa.q: Who helps Bholi gain confidence?
qa.e: Her kind teacher encourages her to speak and learn.

qa.q: Why does Bholi refuse to marry Bishamber at the end?
qa.a: He demands a dowry, showing his greed, and she now has self-respect
qa.e: Education gave her the courage to reject a greedy man.

qa.q: The Right to Education Act, 2009, gives free and compulsory education to children of which age group?
qa.e: The Act covers children from 6 to 14 years.

qa.q: Passage: When Lata joined the village school at nine, she hid behind the last bench. Her teacher, Sunita Ma'am, lent her a picture book every Friday. A year later, Lata read the Republic Day speech aloud to the whole school. What helped Lata change?
qa.e: Sunita Ma'am lent her a picture book every Friday.

qa.q: What should the body of a letter of complaint include?
qa.a: The problem, its details and the action requested
qa.e: A complaint must say what is wrong and what you want done.

qa.q: Which is the best subject line for a complaint letter?
qa.a: Subject: Broken streetlights on the road to the girls' school
qa.e: It is short, specific and states the issue.

qa.q: What does 'illiterate' mean?
qa.e: il- (not) + literate (able to read and write).

qa.q: What difficulty did Bholi have as a child?
qa.e: Her stammer made her shy and the target of teasing.

qa.q: What does Bholi decide to do at the end?
qa.a: Teach at the school where she studied
qa.e: She will care for her parents and teach at her school.

qa.q: Choose the modal: 'You ___ wear a seat belt; it is the law.'
qa.e: A legal rule is a strong obligation: must.

qa.q: Choose the modal: '___ I borrow your pen, please?'
qa.e: 'May' asks for permission politely.

qa.q: Choose the modal: 'She ___ speak three languages fluently.'
qa.e: 'Can' shows ability.

qa.q: Choose the modal: 'You ___ bring lunch; it will be served.'
qa.e: No necessity is shown by 'needn't'.

qa.q: Choose the modal: 'When I was six, I ___ ride a bicycle.'
qa.e: 'Could' is the past form of 'can' for ability.

qa.q: Which word is closest in meaning to 'self-confidence'?
qa.e: Self-assurance means trust in one's own abilities.

qa.q: Who is the leader of the Martians in 'The Book That Saved the Earth'?
qa.e: Think-Tank is the Martians' proud leader.

qa.q: Which book 'saves the Earth' in the play?
qa.a: A book of Mother Goose nursery rhymes
qa.e: The Martians misread nursery rhymes as threats.

qa.q: Why does Think-Tank call off the invasion?
qa.a: He misreads the nursery rhymes as signs of danger
qa.e: He takes harmless rhymes as secret warnings and panics.

qa.q: Who introduces the play?
qa.e: A historian from the future introduces and frames the story.

qa.q: Which is a feature of science fiction?
qa.a: It imagines future science, space travel or other worlds
qa.e: Sci-fi is built on imagined science and technology.

qa.q: What does the root 'tele-' mean?
qa.e: Telephone, television, telescope: all about distance.

qa.q: What does the root 'micro-' mean?
qa.e: Microscope, microchip: very small.

qa.q: What does 'astronaut' literally suggest, from 'astro-'?
qa.e: astro- means star and -naut means sailor: a 'star sailor'.

qa.q: What mainly makes 'The Book That Saved the Earth' funny?
qa.a: The Martians seriously misunderstand simple nursery rhymes
qa.e: Their serious misreading of silly rhymes creates the comedy.

qa.q: Which word best describes Think-Tank?
qa.e: He is very proud of his own mind and keeps insulting Noodle.

qa.q: Who is Think-Tank's apprentice?
qa.e: Noodle is the apprentice whom Think-Tank keeps insulting.

qa.q: The audience knows the rhymes are harmless, but the Martians are terrified. What is this?
qa.e: The audience knows something the characters do not.

qa.q: What is a pun?
qa.a: A play on words using two meanings or similar sounds
qa.e: Puns are jokes based on words with double meanings.

qa.q: Which sentence is a pun?
qa.a: I'm reading a book on anti-gravity; it's impossible to put down.
qa.e: 'Impossible to put down' means both 'very interesting' and 'it floats'.

qa.q: Choose the right word: 'The Martians landed ___, near the library.'
qa.e: 'There' shows a place; 'their' shows possession; 'they're' = they are.

qa.q: What are homophones?
qa.a: Words that sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning
qa.e: Examples: read/reed, knight/night.
